A commit only takes what is staged
`git commit` saves the **staging area**, not your folder. New or changed files go in only after `git add`. (`git commit -a` stages changes to files Git already tracks, but never new files.)
`git add` only puts changes in the staging area (the "next commit" draft). Nothing is in the history until you run `git commit`.
Creating a branch doesn't switch to it

`git branch name` only creates the label; you stay where you are, so the next commit still goes to your current branch. Use `git switch name` afterwards, or create and switch in one go with `git switch -c name`.
Check which branch you're on before committing
Commits go to the branch HEAD points at. Run `git status` (first line: "On branch …") or `git branch` (the `*` marks the current one) before you commit, and `git switch` first if needed.

Git writes both versions into the file between `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>`. Resolving means editing the file into its final form, **deleting those three marker lines**, then `git add` to mark it resolved.
While a merge has conflicts, Git refuses to commit until every conflicted file is fixed **and** staged with `git add`. Then `git commit` finishes the merge.
The hub rejects a push when it has commits you don't (a teammate pushed first). That protects their work. Run `git pull` to bring their commits in (and resolve any conflict), then push again.
Protected `main` only changes through pull requests

The hub refuses direct pushes to a protected branch, with or without `--force`. Put the work on a branch (`git switch -c name`), push the branch (`git push -u origin name`) and open a pull request (`gh pr create`).

`git fetch` downloads new commits and moves `origin/main`, but your own `main` and your files stay as they are. To bring the changes into your branch, merge them (`git merge origin/main`) or use `git pull` (fetch + merge in one step).
The first push of a branch needs -u

A new branch doesn't exist on the hub yet, so Git doesn't know where to push it. `git push -u origin name` creates it there and remembers the link ("upstream"), so later a plain `git push` / `git pull` works.
`restore` undoes uncommitted changes; `revert` undoes a commit

`git restore file` throws away edits you haven't committed (it brings back the staged or committed version). Once a change is committed (and maybe pushed), undo it with `git revert <commit>`: a new commit that does the opposite, so history stays honest.
Plain `git restore file` works on your **folder** (it throws away unstaged edits). To take a file out of the staging area and keep your changes, use `git restore --staged file`.
Merge into the branch you're on

`git merge X` brings X's commits into the **current** branch. To get a feature into main: `git switch main`, then `git merge feature`. Merging main into the feature branch updates the feature branch instead.
`git branch -d` refuses to delete a branch whose commits aren't merged anywhere, so you can't lose work by accident. Merge it first, or use `git branch -D` if you really want to throw it away.
`rm` deletes the file; `git rm` also stages the deletion
After a plain `rm file`, Git sees the file as "deleted" but not yet staged. `git rm file` does both (or run `git add file` after `rm`).
`git init` turns the current folder into a repository. Run it once, inside the project folder. Running it in your home folder (or a parent) makes a repository that swallows everything under it.
